messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hopelessness: I have no future, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mika is a 42-year-old electrician of Pacific Islander background who came to treatment after more than a year of living as though danger could break through an ordinary day without warning. The assault happened at dusk, near the end of a long job. He had been locking up a small commercial site when he heard a door bang behind him and turned too late. What he remembers most clearly are a few sharp pictures: the door swinging open, a man stepping fast into his space, a flash of a raised arm, the concrete coming up toward him. The rest is broken and missing. He cannot put the event into a full sequence, only return to isolated moments that arrive with a physical jolt, and whenever they do he is flooded with guilt, convinced he should have seen it coming or handled it differently.

In the weeks after, dusk became the hardest part of the day. As the light starts to change, Mika feels his body tighten before he has consciously thought about why. The sound of a door opening sharply at a worksite, or slamming in a store, can pull up one of those frozen images so abruptly that for a moment he feels detached and unreal, as if he is no longer fully in the present. In those moments he does not just remember the assault; he lands again in the belief that it says something shameful about him. He has come to believe the attack happened because of the kind of man he is—careless, weak, the sort of person who ends up in that situation when someone better would not have. By evening, especially at the same time of day it happened, his thoughts darken quickly into the sense that nothing ahead of him is likely to improve.

Those meanings have made him live as if vulnerability is visible on him. At work, if someone moves suddenly in the edge of his vision, he jerks back as though bracing for another blow. If a coworker touches his shoulder without warning, he reacts with instant alarm and then embarrassment. He avoids unfamiliar buildings whenever he can, telling himself he needs to know exits and blind spots before he can relax, but underneath is a conviction that he is the kind of person things happen to. The broken, snapshot quality of the memory keeps that danger feeling alive; because he cannot fill in what happened between the fragments, he treats what he cannot remember as further evidence that he was overwhelmed and failed.

Mika has built his evenings around not having to think. When dusk approaches, or when a door bangs and leaves him briefly unreal and shaky, he buries himself in his phone for hours, scrolling, gaming, clicking through anything that can keep his mind occupied. On worse nights he drinks until he feels dulled enough not to see the pictures so vividly. He has stopped watching films or shows with assaults or tense confrontations because he knows how quickly they can set him off. The same happens when the memory intrudes on its own: once the images start, and the guilt comes with them, he reaches for a screen or alcohol to push them away.

These habits have narrowed his life and deepened the conclusions he draws about himself. He is less present with his partner in the evenings, sitting beside her but absorbed in his phone or drinking past conversation. He feels ashamed of how much time disappears this way, and that shame confirms his hopelessness: in his mind, a man who has to manage himself like this is not someone with much of a future. The drinking and constant distraction also leave him less grounded, so the next day he is more keyed up, more likely to react to sudden movement or touch, and more dependent on scanning whether a place feels safe enough to enter.

Over time, the strategies meant to keep the assault out of mind have made the triggers more central in his life. He organizes routes and jobs to avoid unfamiliar places, but that means doors slamming at the sites he does attend, and the approach of dusk on every workday, stand out even more. He notices the time constantly. He has begun to dread the first hint of feeling detached, because he takes that sensation itself as a sign that he is slipping back toward the assault and toward those same accusing thoughts about what sort of person he is. When he finally sought help, it was after snapping away from a coworker who touched him unexpectedly and then sitting in his truck after work, unable to face going into another building. What frightened him most was the sense that his world was shrinking around a handful of moments he could not fully remember, and what he hopes for is simple: to get through the end of the day without feeling that the assault is still waiting for him.
